body: stack-docker-unreached-at-start: Evidence, re-verified at the tree as it stands; the filed problem has not rotted. plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/stack:start_run probes docker once, at line 729 (`reached = docker_reached(shutil.which("docker"))`), before it spawns the holder and runs the start command at 734, and records the answer on the entry through record_holder. stack:docker_reached (581-589) runs `docker version --format {{.Server.Version}}` and emits STACK.DOCKER.UNREACHED on failure. stack:docker_out_of_reach (592-593) is `entry.get("docker") is False and not docker_reached(docker)`. stack:removal_steps (638-652) skips remove_docker where docker_out_of_reach holds, reporting "docker's daemon answered neither when the run started nor now", and returns no docker refusal, so take_down settles the entry as fully removed and deletes it. stack:in_use (816-838) skips the running-container check on the same test. Mechanism: a start command that starts the daemon, makes labelled objects, and then has the daemon stop before `down` leaves objects that carry the run's label with no registry entry, so no later `cleanup` finds them. The skip came from certification defect i17 (run converge-2026-10-15T011914): without it, a run that made no docker object, taken down while Docker Desktop is installed and stopped, kept its entry and its leased ports, and every later cleanup refused it again. Corpus: decision:run-artifacts-recorded-by-the-stack-tool says "`down` removes every container, image, volume, and network that carries it" and is silent on an unreachable daemon; decision:stack-tool-runs-each-run says `down` "deletes the entry once every removal succeeds"; decision:run-artifacts-removed-with-the-run says "A removal docker refuses leaves the entry in place with the refusal named"; story:verification-leaves-no-artifacts-behind owes that a run's artifacts are removed once it is over. None says what counts as a removal when docker cannot be reached. Harm: labelled objects stay on disk with nothing that records them; no accept-list entry covers it as a defect (the report line is honest, so not A9), so this is the owner's choice. Options: A. The answer before the start command decides (the code now); corpus records it; cost: a start command that starts and then loses the daemon leaves labelled objects with no record. B. Probe before and after the start command, skip docker at `down` only where neither probe and the `down` probe answered; cost: one more docker call per `stack up`, and a daemon started and stopped inside the start command still escapes. C. The answer at `down` alone decides, and the entry drops; cost: any run that made labelled objects loses its entry while the daemon is stopped. D (the filer missed it). Where the daemon does not answer at `down`, release the ports and stop the group and delete the folder, but keep the entry marked docker-pending so a later `cleanup` removes its labelled objects once the daemon answers; cost: on a machine where docker is installed and never started, pending entries accumulate and `list` shows them, and decision:run-artifacts-removed-with-the-run's "deletes the entry once every removal succeeds" must name the pending state. Every option but A edits the decisions named above. Siblings from the same certification run: stack-tag-variable-collision-key, true-up-payload-copy-detection.

stack-tag-variable-collision-key: Evidence, re-verified at the tree as it stands; the filed problem has not rotted. plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/stack:stack_defects (288-321) and plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/plumbline:stackDefects (297-329) both print 'stack.tag_variable "<NAME>" is also a name ports declares, and the stack tool sets it to the run tag' when a declared port name equals stack.tag_variable. plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/true-up:config_named_keys (2778-2779) names each key in CONFIG_CHECK_KEYS whose name opens a defect (`d.startswith(key)`), so the offer names `stack`; true-up:changed_keys (2782-2794) refuses a draft that changes any key not named, so a port rename is refused as "ports (changed)". plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/ADMINISTRATION.md:122 says `resolve` refuses a `config` draft that "adds, drops, or changes a key the offer does not name". Mechanism: which key the offer accepts follows from the first word of the defect text alone; certification defect i16 (run converge-2026-10-15T011914) re-worded the text to open with `stack` and recorded the choice as question call i29, on the reasoning that a port rename reaches every compose file and command that reads the port variable, while tag_variable is read by the start command alone. Corpus: decision:stack-ports-checked-as-a-suite-rule binds host ports to declared port names and is silent on tag_variable; no artifact under .ok-planner/design/ names tag_variable. story:true-up-project-estate owes that upgrading never costs the owner work they wrote. The change lies in the project's own tooling (the defect text in stack and plumbline, the offer in true-up, ADMINISTRATION.md:122). No accept-list entry covers either reading; this is the owner's choice. Options: A. A stack defect (the code now): ADMINISTRATION.md says the owner repairs it by choosing another tag_variable; cost: an owner who would rather rename the port edits the config by hand. B. A ports defect: the defect text opens with `ports` again in both copies, and the offer refuses a tag_variable change; cost: the rename reaches every compose file and command that reads the port variable. C. Both keys: config_named_keys names both `stack` and `ports` for this one defect; cost: the one offer where a defect names two keys, and a special case in config_named_keys beside the prefix rule. Siblings from the same certification run: stack-docker-unreached-at-start, true-up-payload-copy-detection.

true-up-payload-copy-detection: Evidence, re-verified at the tree as it stands; the filed problem has not rotted. plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/true-up:payload_copy_file (1903-1909) walks each parent folder of a file and returns True where the folder holds both admin/true-up and admin/ADMINISTRATION.md; true-up:caller_kind (1912-1932) returns no caller kind for such a file, so it is never repointed, never gets an intake issue, and never holds a retired script copy back. plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/ADMINISTRATION.md:247 states the same skip: "a file of a family payload that sits inside the project, as in the suite's own repository: the payload that runs true-up, or any folder below the project root holding both admin/true-up and admin/ADMINISTRATION.md". Mechanism: certification defect i19 (run converge-2026-10-15T011914) added the skip because /ok in this repository runs the installed payload from the plugin cache, so the in-tree copy at plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/ is not the payload that runs true-up, and its own documentation of .ok-planner/bin/run-tag and .ok-planner/bin/port-block drew false caller issues that kept both retired copies for good; the fixer recorded the choice as question call i31. Corpus: decision:retired-script-repoint-needs-a-proven-root says "removing the copy behind it can break a real caller, so holding the copy and asking the owner costs only a kept file", and is silent on payload copies; story:true-up-project-estate owes that upgrading never costs the owner work they wrote. No artifact under .ok-planner/design/ names a payload copy. The change lies in the project's own tooling (true-up and ADMINISTRATION.md:247), with option C also adding a config key. No accept-list entry covers either reading; this is the owner's choice. Options: A. Two administration files mark a payload copy (the code now); cost: a project file below such a folder that calls a retired script is never flagged, and true-up removes the copy it calls, which the decision's rationale names as the harm to avoid. B. Only the payload that runs true-up is skipped; cost: the suite's own repository gets a false caller issue for each retired script its payload documents and keeps each retired copy until the owner answers. C. The project declares its payload copies in .ok-planner/config.json; cost: a config key only the suite's own repository uses, with config-check and the config offer to extend. D (the filer missed it). Skip a file below such a folder only where the running payload carries a file at the same path relative to the folder, so a project file the payload does not carry still counts as a caller; cost: a file the working tree's payload adds before the installed release carries it draws a false caller issue until the next release. Siblings from the same certification run: stack-docker-unreached-at-start, stack-tag-variable-collision-key.

plumbline-prescribes-no-home-for-shared-code: Evidence, re-verified at the tree as it stands. The rules the issue quotes still read as filed: plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/docs/plumbline-coding.md:66-72, section 6 "Import, never copy", step 1 "Where it exists, import it" and step 2 "Where a dependency-split rule seems to block the import, read what the module actually imports before assuming"; plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/docs/plumbline-cheatsheet.md:23 "layering → dependency lint" and its "Strict DRY: semantically identical logic lives in ONE place". No rule in either file tells a project to declare a layer order, says which way an import may point, or names a function-local import placed to dodge a circular-import error. The lint checks five things and no import graph: plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/plumbline:182-190 LINT_CHECK_NAMES is comment-hygiene, citation-resolution, no-tests, compose-ports, compose-labels. The LineScout evidence (linescout/platform, package gridiq: one 12-unit import cycle, three 2-unit cycles, 13 function-local imports, 12 root modules importing service packages) comes from another project and cannot be re-verified from this tree; the brief takes it as the owner's report. Mechanism: step 1 points the agent at wherever the function already sits, and step 2 weighs an import's weight, never its direction, so in a multi-package project each reuse can add an edge up or across, and nothing mechanical refuses the cycle. Where the change lies: the canonical rule sources and the lint are the project's own shipped product (.ok-planner/review/project.md:7 names plugins/ as the shipped product), so this is not upstream; the materialized copies under .claude/rules/ change only by /ok. Corpus: concept:cheatsheet says the rules layer is "the small, stable, condensed statement of the suite's rules", so new rule text costs context residency; decision:project-chooses-its-lint-checks enumerates the five lint checks and says turning a check off drops its rule text, so a new check edits that decision; decision:stack-ports-checked-as-a-suite-rule is the precedent for a suite rule a project checks "with the suite's lint where the lint applies, with a project lint, or with both". No artifact under .ok-planner/design/ speaks to import direction or layering. No accept-list entry covers this; it asks what the product prescribes, so it is the owner's choice. Options: A. Prose rules only: amend section 6 step 2 to weigh direction, and add rules that shared code moves down to the lowest package both callers may import, and that a function-local import placed to dodge a cycle is a defect fixed by moving the code; cost: a written constraint with no check, against the cheatsheet's "Every written constraint needs a check that fails on violation". B. Prose rules plus a suite lint check: a declared layer order in .ok-planner/config.json and a new check in scripts/plumbline that fails an import against it; cost: per-language import parsing in a lint that today reads comments and compose files, a new config key with config-check and a true-up config offer, and amendments to decision:project-chooses-its-lint-checks. C. Prose rules plus a project-checked layering rule, after the stack-ports precedent: the suite states the rule and that a project declares its layer order and checks it with a project lint (an import linter for its language); cost: a project with no such lint gets only text, and the suite cannot check the wiring. D. Leave layering to each project's subjects and practices; cost: the reuse rule keeps sending agents across package boundaries until an owner writes a practice. Siblings: none open.
